findings.description: Critical: D1 specifies `ExecutionAdapter.route_parked_escalations(workspace, batch_id, repo_root, evaluator=None)` as a new adapter method that reloads the checkpoint, but never states its locking discipline — and the sibling pattern it will be written to match self-deadlocks. Every other durable adapter method (`prepare`, `child_start`, `acknowledge`, `reconcile`, `resume`, `apply`) carries `@_serialized_transition` (skills/supervise/scripts/execution.py:133-141), which calls `_state_lock` (execution.py:116-131). `_state_lock` does a fresh `os.open` and `fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX)` on every entry; flock locks are held by the open file description, not the process, so a second acquisition from the same process on a new descriptor blocks on the first rather than being granted. Routing calls `gate_router.resolve_parked` (gate_router.py:654-659), which on PROCEED calls `adapter.resume` — itself `@_serialized_transition` (execution.py:856). A decorated `route_parked_escalations` therefore hangs the supervise session forever on the very first auto-posture escalation, with the attempt durably parked and the host blocked mid-cycle (no timeout, no error, nothing to retry). This is a code-level trace of the existing lock helper, not an executed run — the sandbox declined to run Python here.
findings.resolution: State the lock contract in D1: `route_parked_escalations` MUST NOT be decorated with `_serialized_transition`; it performs an unlocked read of durable state and delegates every mutation to `resume`, which takes the lock itself. Add a note that any future adapter method calling into `gate_router` inherits the same constraint, and add a bounded (timeout-guarded) test that an auto-posture policy pause routes and resumes to completion — the current Test Strategy item 1 would hang rather than fail if this is gotten wrong.

findings.description: Critical: making routing automatic converts the router's dispatch-scoped prior-record rule into an unbounded auto-resume loop with no human in it. The escalate_resume subject key is `(gate, roadmap_id, dispatch_id)` (gate_router.py:152-157), and `resume` preserves `dispatch_id`, `attempt`, and `launch_token`, incrementing only `lease_generation` (execution.py:889-906). `_apply_prior_record` returns a reused decision immediately for any prior `outcome == "proceed"` without consulting the posture (gate_router.py:462-463), and `resolve_parked` then calls `adapter.resume` on every reuse — the existing test asserts exactly this and comments it: "resume() is still called each time; only evaluation is deduped" (skills/tests/supervise/test_gate_router.py:592). `require_approval_ref` accepts the same stale `gate-decision:<id>` because gate, outcome, and dispatch_id all still match (gate_router.py:705-723). So once escalate_resume proceeds once for a dispatch, every subsequent ESCALATE of that same dispatch auto-resumes off the original record: escalate → auto-resume → child re-runs and exhausts its budget → escalate → auto-resume, forever, never re-reading TRUST_POSTURE.md and never reaching a coordinator, each cycle costing a full child dispatch. Under today's manual reconciliation this needed a human to re-trigger each pass; the change removes that damper and the plan adds no bound. The spec's 'Repeated reconciliation' scenario only covers re-routing the *same* park, not a second park of the same dispatch.
findings.resolution: Bound escalate_resume explicitly. Either include the parked generation in the subject key (e.g. `(gate, roadmap_id, dispatch_id, lease_generation)`) so each new escalation is a fresh decision subject, or cap escalate_resume proceeds per `dispatch_id` and fail closed to blocked past the cap. Add a spec scenario and a RED test for the second policy_pause on an already-resumed dispatch, asserting it does not silently reuse the earlier proceed.

findings.description: Critical: the plan verifies resume up to the generation increment and stops, but the resumed generation appears unable to ever have its next result applied — so the acceptance outcome 'the exhausted dispatch resumed' can pass while the item can never complete. `ExecutionAdapter.resume` pops `lease`, `launch_evidence`, `launch_gate`, `parked`, `quarantine`, `outcome`, `resolved_at`, `handoff_id` but leaves `application_journal` in place (execution.py:893-903), still at `effects_applied` and bound to the previous result. The resumed attempt keeps its original `dispatch_id`, hence its original `batch_id` prefix, and `prepare_delegated_batch` excludes items with an unresolved attempt status — `prepared` is one (orchestrator.py:162-165) — so no new batch can ever carry it. Re-applying the original batch reaches `_bound_application_journal(attempt, result)` in the pre-pass (orchestrator.py:643, helper at 522-535), which compares the stored journal result against the new one; they always differ (at minimum `lease_generation`), so it raises 'bound dispatch result mismatch'. No existing test applies a batch after a resume — test_execution.py:942 stops at `enter` — so this dead end is currently unobserved. ri-06 puts it on the critical path by making proceed-resume the automatic outcome of every auto-posture escalation.
findings.resolution: Add a task and an end-to-end test covering the full loop: park → route → proceed → child_start/acknowledge/enter → apply the new result. If it fails as traced, resume must clear or rebind `application_journal` alongside the other per-generation fields, and the change should say so in the design rather than leaving it to the implementer to discover mid-TDD.

findings.description: Nit: the artifacts disagree on where the resolution list surfaces, which is precisely the boundary this change's retry-safety argument rests on. The spec scenario says 'the bounded **apply result** reports the correlated escalation resolution', and contracts/README.md:3 says 'The observable Python return value adds a bounded `escalation_resolutions` list while preserving existing keys' — both read as an addition to `ExecutionAdapter.apply`'s return. Design D4 (design.md:23) and task 2.3 (tasks.md:14) say the opposite: apply and all its existing return keys are unchanged, and resolutions come from `route_parked_escalations`. A conformant implementation would fail the spec as written; an implementation satisfying the spec would break the stated compatibility guarantee.
findings.resolution: Reword the scenario bullet to name the routing operation ('the routing operation returns a bounded resolution entry for the correlated dispatch, without child transcript content') and rewrite contracts/README.md to attribute `escalation_resolutions` to `route_parked_escalations`, restating that `apply`'s return shape is unchanged.

findings.description: Nit: D5 covers routing failing after a successful apply, but not apply failing after durable parking — which reintroduces exactly the defect the change exists to remove. `apply_delegated_batch` persists per attempt and saves incrementally inside its loop (orchestrator.py:656-758), so a later member raising ('dispatch outcome mismatch', 'dispatch replan mismatch', a roadmap save error) leaves an earlier member's policy_pause durably parked with its lease released while `apply` propagates the exception. The host, following D1's 'immediately after it succeeds', never routes that attempt, so the escalation again waits for a later session to happen to discover it.
findings.resolution: Specify that routing keys off durable state rather than off apply's return: the host runs `route_parked_escalations(batch_id)` after apply whether apply returned or raised, and the operation is safe (idempotent, scan-based) in both cases. Add a test that applies a two-member batch where the second member raises and asserts the first member's policy_pause still routes.

findings.description: Optional: the notify-with-timeout scenario specifies the notification window but no bound on the routing call itself. `ApprovalGate.evaluate` under notify_with_timeout files, notifies, then blocks in `while self.clock() < deadline` polling `check_approval` until the human answers or `timeout_seconds` elapses (skills/shared/approval_gate.py:459-483). Routing runs synchronously in the supervise host immediately after apply, one attempt at a time, so a batch with N parked escalations blocks the session for up to N × timeout_seconds with no stated ceiling. Under the current manual path a human chose when to pay that cost; the change makes it mandatory at every failure boundary.
findings.resolution: State the wall-clock contract in the spec: a per-attempt bound of the gate's own `timeout_seconds` and an explicit statement of whether routing is sequential over the batch, so an operator can predict the worst case from posture alone. Consider requiring all filings before any polling, or documenting the total budget in SKILL.md alongside the retry instruction.

findings.description: Nit: task 2.1 says the method 'reloads the checkpoint' and scans it, but does not constrain what it may do with that in-memory copy — and the natural read-modify-write shape corrupts the audit trail. `gate_router.evaluate` builds its own `CheckpointManager`, appends via `record_gate_decision`, and rewrites the whole document (checkpoint.py:98-114, 55-62); `resume` does the same through `_load_attempt`. A routing method that keeps its scan-time `Checkpoint` object across those calls and later saves it would silently clobber the gate-decision records the router just wrote, and a scan-time status snapshot would let an attempt already resumed by an interleaved path be routed a second time.
findings.resolution: Require in D1/task 2.1 that the routing method never calls `manager.save` itself and re-reads each attempt's durable status immediately before its `resolve_parked` call. Add an assertion to the idempotency test that the gate-decision record written during routing is present in checkpoint.json after the call returns.

findings.description: Nit: task 3.1 will edit SKILL.md into a structural guard the plan never mentions. `test_prose_free_gates.py::test_every_gate_name_sits_in_a_protocol_block` fails if `escalate_resume` appears anywhere in skills/supervise/SKILL.md outside a fenced block containing `gate-check`, `gate-answer`, or `resolve_parked` (marker list at test_prose_free_gates.py:93), and the module docstring records the deliberate invariant that supervise documents this gate generically — today's prose says 'the ESCALATE-resume gate' for exactly that reason (SKILL.md:396). A new fenced block showing only `adapter.route_parked_escalations(...)` is not recognised as a protocol block, so naming the gate near it fails the suite. Test Strategy item 4 lists only the pending_gate/failed/quarantine guards.
findings.resolution: Add a task bullet: keep the routing documentation gate-name-free, or extend `_protocol_blocks`' marker list to include the new method deliberately (and record that in the design). Either way the guard must be updated intentionally, not weakened to make the doc edit pass.

findings.description: Optional: the requirement's load-bearing clause — 'the host SHALL immediately invoke its retryable parked-escalation operation' — has no executable verification anywhere in the plan. The new tests exercise the method in isolation; nothing asserts the host actually calls it after apply, so the whole change can regress to the status quo (routing only when a later session notices) with a green suite. The repo has direct precedent for pinning host sequencing in the document: `test_workflow_contract.py` already asserts the collect/apply and ack/go orderings from SKILL.md prose.
findings.resolution: Add a task and a `test_workflow_contract.py` assertion that the 'Collect and apply' section pins the routing call immediately after apply and documents retrying only the routing method — mirroring `test_execute_pins_the_ack_go_entry_sequence`.

findings.description: Optional: D4 bounds what routing returns but says nothing about what it sends. `resolve_parked` puts the child's `parked.reason` into the evaluation context (gate_router.py:641-647), and `ApprovalGate._notify` forwards that whole context to the coordinator via `request_approval(context=ctx)` and interpolates it into the notification body (`parts.append(f"Context: {ctx}")`, approval_gate.py:435-451, 676-686). The reason is bounded and schema-validated (≤1024 chars, execution.py:420-433) but not scrubbed — `_SECRET_KEY` filtering applies to dispatch-context *keys*, never to this value. This change makes that the first automatic outbound path at a phase-failure boundary, which is where a reason is most likely to carry error or log text.
findings.resolution: State the outbound contract in the design: the escalate_resume filing carries only `{dispatch_id, change_id, item_id, verb}` plus the already-bounded `parked.reason`, never evidence, loop-state, or transcript content. Add an assertion to the notify-with-timeout test on the exact context the fake coordinator receives.

findings.description: Optional: task 3.2 tells the implementer to run `skills/install.sh`, but the package's `write_allow` only permits `.claude/skills/supervise/**` and `.agents/skills/supervise/**`. install.sh has no per-skill mode — `--agents` selects harness roots, not skills — so it rsyncs every portable skill's runtime mirror. If any other mirror is already stale, the run writes outside the declared scope and trips the write audit for a reason unrelated to this change.
findings.resolution: Either narrow 3.2 to 'verify byte identity of the supervise runtime mirrors against skills/supervise/, syncing only those files', or widen `write_allow` to `.claude/skills/**` and `.agents/skills/**` with a note that install.sh is repo-wide by design.

findings.description: FYI: the Why frames the defect as routing happening 'only when a later session happens to discover the parked attempt', but the fix is scoped to the named batch (D1), so any attempt parked in an earlier batch — or parked in this one when the session dies before routing completes — still falls back to exactly that discovery path via SKILL.md's existing 'Reconcile and resume' section. That is a defensible boundary given the retry-safety argument, but it is currently unstated, so a reader could conclude the discovery gap is closed in general.
findings.resolution: Add one line to Out of Scope: sweeping previously parked attempts from earlier batches remains the existing manual reconcile path; this change guarantees immediate routing only for the batch just applied.

findings.description: Three of the review's target guarantees hold as specified and are worth recording as verified. (a) Exclusions are structural, not conventional: filtering on durable `status == "parked"` plus `parked.kind == "policy_pause"` cannot reach a `pending_gate` (different kind), a failure (status `failed`), or a quarantine (status `quarantined`, which `resume` refuses outright at execution.py:871-872). (b) Post-parking ordering is real: `_terminal_attempt` sets `status="parked"`, `lease.state="released"`, and advances the journal to `terminal_persisted` with a save before effects (orchestrator.py:588-610, 716-720), so routing after apply always sees a durably parked, lease-released attempt. (c) The mirror/handoff guarantee needs no schema work: `escalate_resume` is already in the `gate` enum of both supervisor-record.schema.json and supervisor-record-mirror.schema.json, `approval_id` is nullable, `_clean_pending_gate` preserves `deadline`, `disposition`, and `decision_id` (cycle_state.py:236-273), and `_durable_sections` expires standing decisions but never pending gates (cycle_state.py:390-404), so a blocked escalate_resume entry survives rehydration with its computed deadline. Separately, the D5 apply/route split is belt-and-braces rather than the sole protection: the application journal already makes `dispatch_fn` at-most-once per generation (orchestrator.py:682-695, 722-723), so even a mistaken `apply` retry could not replay the callback.
findings.resolution: No change required; consider citing the journal's independent at-most-once guarantee in D5 so the retry-safety argument does not rest solely on the call split.
